title: Part 1
text: A whale has just landed on the deep seafloor, and the guests are arriving. Meet the first three.

title: Part 2
text: Among the first big visitors are sharks. Pacific sleeper sharks have been filmed feeding on whale carcasses on the seafloor.
nxt: These sluggish, ancient-looking predators bite into thick blubber and shake their bodies to tear off chunks of flesh.

title: Part 3
text: Joining the sharks are hagfish, primitive jawless fish from a lineage that has lasted hundreds of millions of years.
nxt: With no true jaws, they rasp flesh away with toothlike plates made of keratin. Hagfish can burrow right into a carcass and eat it from the inside out.

title: Part 4
text: Then come the crustaceans. Giant isopods, armored cousins of the pill bugs in your garden, can grow longer than thirty centimeters and are known for swarming carcasses on the deep seafloor.
nxt: They can survive long stretches without food, so when a feast finally arrives, they make the most of it.

title: Part 5
text: This stage is astonishingly fast, even in the cold and the dark.
nxt: Researchers estimate that scavengers can strip forty to sixty kilograms of soft tissue from a carcass every single day.

title: Part 6
text: With the big scavengers gone, the whale fall enters its second phase, the opportunistic stage, which lasts for months to a few years.
nxt: The target now is not big chunks of meat, but the scraps scattered across the surrounding mud.
